name: Market socialism
summary: Market socialism holds that the means of production should be socially owned, by the public or by the workers who use them, while goods, services and usually capital goods are exchanged in competitive markets. Its theorists reject both capitalist ownership, with its unearned property income and concentrated wealth, and Soviet-style central planning, which they regard as inefficient and authoritarian. Most modern designs pair self-managed or publicly owned firms with public banks or public control over new investment, and aim at greater equality, workplace democracy and political democracy.
scope: The theoretical family as defined by its main designers: Lange's 1936-38 competitive-socialism model, Nove's feasible socialism, Roemer's coupon socialism and Bardhan and Roemer's bank-centric model, Miller's cooperative market socialism, and above all Schweickart's Economic Democracy, with Mill as forerunner and Yugoslav workers' self-management (1950 Basic Law, Tito) as its main historical experiment. Where the state-owned (Lange, Roemer, Nove) and cooperative (Mill, Schweickart, Yugoslav) strands differ, answers are 0 or low. China's and Vietnam's socialist market economies and Proudhonian mutualism are excluded; outside economics most answers are low-confidence inferences.

sources.usedFor: Three features of the model (self-managed firms, markets, social control of investment via capital-assets tax and public banks); rejection of central planning; political democracy presupposed; interest unnecessary; labour not a commodity; alienation; legislatures setting product and technology standards; lessons from Yugoslavia and Mondragon.

sources.title: Economic Democracy: An Ethically Desirable Socialism That Is Economically Viable (Next System Project, 2015)
sources.author: David Schweickart
sources.usedFor: The model's three features and extensions (employer of last resort, socialist protectionism, entrepreneurial sector), and Schweickart's answers on planning, trade, inequality, environment, liberty, transition and politics.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Schweickart keeps markets as a necessary part of viable socialism, with prices set by supply and demand and income as shares of profit, which keeps money in use.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Schweickart says his model replaces most wage labour with cooperative labour, yet allows small and large entrepreneurial capitalist firms that still hire workers.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Schweickart says productivity gains can be taken as leisure rather than output in democratic firms and that Keynes's short working week could be reached under Economic Democracy.

ban-interest.rationale: Schweickart explicitly allows socialist savings and loan associations, as credit unions or cooperatives, to lend to individuals and pay savers interest.

capital-controls.rationale: Schweickart has investment funds raised by taxation and required by law to be reinvested in domestic firms, so that capital is not exported.

central-planning.rationale: Schweickart states that central planning does not work for a sophisticated economy because of its knowledge and incentive problems, and the Stanford Encyclopedia reports market socialism as a response to central planning's inefficiency and concentration of power.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Schweickart's basic value is participatory autonomy, the right of individuals to take part in forming the rules to which they must submit.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Schweickart says the planet cannot sustain ever more mindless consumption and expects consumerism to wither in Economic Democracy.

corporate-influence.rationale: Schweickart says the dominant economic class controls almost the whole political process and the major media, and wants Citizens United reversed.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Schweickart has the government guarantee a job to everyone and provide free health care, education, childcare and retirement income, so poverty would be virtually eliminated.

decide-locally.rationale: Schweickart sends investment funds to regions and communities by per-capita right and expects glocalization, but keeps national planning for national projects and says the aim is a balance between coordinated planning and local autonomy.

democracy-best.rationale: Schweickart calls for extending democracy to the workplace and to investment and for democratizing democracy, while conceding that democratic institutions yield bad outcomes if a majority holds bad values.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Schweickart envisages a democratic, nonviolent restructuring carried out by a political movement that wins political power, with entrepreneurial capitalists keeping an honourable role, not a class dictatorship.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Schweickart calls climate change an urgent reason for democratic control of investment, says fundamental change must be well underway within a decade or two, and gives government the tasks of regulation and investment for sustainability.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: Schweickart includes free health care, education and childcare in his model, funded from general taxes.

free-trade.rationale: Schweickart adopts fair trade, not free trade: free trade only with countries of comparable wages and regulations, social tariffs against race-to-the-bottom competition.

future-generations.rationale: Schweickart ties the need for a new economic system to the prospects of our children and grandchildren and names ecological sustainability as overriding.

harm-principle.rationale: Schweickart says liberty includes people living as they see fit so long as they do not harm others, in accordance with the harm principle Mill advocated.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Schweickart replaces the interest and dividends paid to owners of capital with a capital-assets tax, and treats the capitalist's passive role as a supplier of capital as the basic problem, while workers share in profits.

job-guarantee.rationale: Schweickart states that everyone who wants to work should have a genuine right to work, and the government will ensure it by acting as employer of last resort.

limit-growth.rationale: Schweickart argues that GDP growth should play no role in investment decisions, quotes Boulding that exponential growth cannot continue in a finite world, and says Economic Democracy need not grow relentlessly.

means-match-ends.rationale: Schweickart says the transition requires a mass movement embracing values and behaviours consonant with the aim, and that new values spread through people acting on them.

moral-incentives.rationale: Schweickart says every worker's income is tied directly to the firm's performance, so that there is incentive to work diligently, rather than relying on social duty alone.

municipal-property.rationale: Schweickart places ownership of cooperative firms with the national state, which leases them to workers, or with the workers themselves, not with the local community.

nation-first.rationale: Schweickart says socialist protectionism protects domestic workers so as to improve life prospects everywhere, not at the expense of workers abroad, and commits an Economic Democracy to join international agreements on poverty and climate.

natural-rulers.rationale: Schweickart's basic value is participatory autonomy, the right of individuals to take part in forming the rules they must obey, which cannot sit with a class naturally fitted to rule.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Schweickart rejects capitalism and says Soviet-style central planning does not work, offering a third, market-based and democratic socialism, and the Stanford Encyclopedia presents market socialism as the response to problems of central planning.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Schweickart gives government the roles of investment financing, employer of last resort, regulation and welfare services, and says government is absolutely essential.

one-party-rule.rationale: Schweickart's model rests on a democratic government with legislatures at national and regional level and a transition won by a political movement contending for power, which excludes exclusive party rule.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: Schweickart expects a political movement to win through the political process the power to nationalize banking and grant workers control, and the reviewer describes his transition as an elected radical government's reforms.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Participatory autonomy is Schweickart's basic value, and he extends democratic participation to the workplace and to the yearly choice of how local investment funds are used.

production-for-use.rationale: Schweickart states that the profit motive plays a fundamental role in the day-to-day allocation of resources and that firms' income depends on profitability, so profit stays the driver of production.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Schweickart says capitalists' income depends on paying workers less than the value they create, which he calls worker exploitation, and calls their passive role as suppliers of capital parasitic; he exempts active entrepreneurs.

public-ownership.rationale: Schweickart says most ownership of the means of production in Economic Democracy is collective, with the state owning cooperative firms and leasing them to their workers; the Stanford Encyclopedia describes the state leasing means of production in his model.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Schweickart requires firms to comply with health, safety and environmental regulations and wants the government authorised to protect the ecosystem by regulation; he does not describe the rules as strict.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Schweickart acknowledges a human obligation to eliminate poverty everywhere and proposes rebating the tariff proceeds to poorer countries, freely sharing intellectual property and research.

simple-living.rationale: Schweickart quotes Thoreau's call for simplicity approvingly, expects workers to choose leisure over needless consumption and says the planet cannot sustain ever more mindless consumption.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Schweickart says implementing Economic Democracy would not require constitutional change and describes the transition as democratic and nonviolent, working through existing political institutions.

social-market-economy.rationale: Schweickart describes a market economy for goods and services together with free health care, education and a job guarantee, with welfare services at least as extensive as the Nordic countries.

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: Schweickart envisages the transition to Economic Democracy as a democratic, nonviolent restructuring of economic institutions.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Schweickart presents Economic Democracy as a model for a single national economy, protected by fair-trade tariffs, and does not make it depend on revolutions elsewhere.

socialized-markets.rationale: Economic Democracy keeps competitive markets for goods and services and replaces most wage labour with cooperative labour, which is exactly a market economy of worker-run firms.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Social control of investment is one of the three defining features: legislatures set national, regional and local investment priorities and public banks lend the investment fund accordingly, although the text does not speak of strategic industries by name.

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: In Schweickart's model public banks lend the investment fund to enterprises, mostly worker self-managed, and he supports technical and financial support for cooperative start-ups.

state-harmful.rationale: Schweickart calls a genuinely democratic government absolutely essential to reach and keep a just and sustainable society, and gives the state the task of generating and steering investment.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Schweickart's model rests on democratic government and a transition won by an open political movement, and he criticises capitalism for undermining rule by the people, so suppressing opposition contradicts it.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Schweickart proposes a social tariff on imports from countries with low wages or lax social and environmental rules, to block race-to-the-bottom competition, while allowing free trade with comparable countries.

taxation-theft.rationale: Schweickart funds the investment fund with a capital-assets tax and government expenses with a separate income or consumption tax, and treats the capital tax as a lease fee for social property.

total-state.rationale: Schweickart keeps markets for goods and services, puts firms under workers' control and bases liberty on participatory autonomy, which excludes a state directing every area of life.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Schweickart ties trade to wage and social and environmental standards through a social tariff on imports from countries whose standards are lower.

unions-good.rationale: Schweickart calls organized labour essential to moving beyond capitalism and says it has a key role in democratizing the workplace and capital.

unions-run-economy.rationale: Schweickart has workers' councils run firms and legislatures steer investment, and says the labour movement should aspire to make itself unnecessary.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Schweickart lists free health care among the guarantees that remove basic economic insecurity in Economic Democracy, alongside free education, childcare and retirement income.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Schweickart states that massive economic inequality has compromised the political system and made a mockery of rule by the people, and that the wealthy class controls the political process and the media.

worker-ownership.rationale: Mill expected associations of labourers collectively owning their capital and Schweickart has workers control their firms, leasing the capital from the state or owning shares in it, so ownership is collective in either form.

workers-councils.rationale: Schweickart places political decisions in national and regional legislatures and puts workers' councils at the level of the firm, not in place of parliaments.

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: Schweickart says a committed political movement should champion intermediate reforms that move toward a democratic economy, such as support for cooperative start-ups and state public banks.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Schweickart makes workplace democracy one of three defining features, with a worker council elected by one-person-one-vote that appoints upper management; Mill also expected managers elected and removable by the workers.

missingStatements.text: The allocation of new investment should be publicly controlled.
missingStatements.rationale: Social control of investment through a capital-assets tax and public banks is one of the three defining features of Schweickart's model, stated in his own outline and in his short statement of it.

quotes.text: Let us generate our investment funds publicly via a capital-assets tax: a flat-rate property tax on all businesses.
quotes.where: p. 4, "The Basic Model", social control of investment

quotes.text: Funds for new investment are generated by a capital assets tax and are returned to the economy through a network of public investment banks.
quotes.where: Economic Democracy, summary of the three features

notes: Strands differ mainly on who holds firms (state or public agencies in Lange, Roemer and Nove; workers in Mill, Schweickart and Yugoslavia) and on interest, which Schweickart would largely abolish but other designs keep. Yugoslav self-management operated under one-party rule, while the modern theorists presuppose multiparty democracy; the profile follows the modern theorists on political questions. Lange later moved toward a mixed public-private economy. Primary books by Lange, Nove, Roemer and Miller could not be opened online, so their positions are cited through scholarly reviews and summaries. Later pass 2026-11-13 (queued for misapplied family approach): answers now rest on the strand's own statements, chiefly Schweickart's 2015 outline of Economic Democracy (s16, answering a questionnaire on economy, society, environment, polity, trade and transition) with Mill and the scholarship; answers that rested only on what adherents or the model's silence suggested, or on Wikipedia, were nulled with the old versions kept in reviewHistory. Schweickart's 1992 article (s1) and the Mises review of Roemer (s10) could not be re-opened (host gone; 403), so no current answer cites them. Themes searched: ownership, markets and planning, investment, labour and unions, welfare, trade, environment, liberty, democracy and transition; foreign policy, religion, gender, culture and law-and-order are not addressed by the defining sources (Schweickart says his work does not address foreign policy).
